analysis.one_liner: Requires health plans to cover at least 48 hours of hospital care after a mastectomy.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to a House committee and never received a vote before Congress adjourned in January 1997.
analysis.plain_summary: In the mid-1990s, health insurers were pressing women to leave the hospital within hours of a mastectomy — so-called 'drive-through' mastectomies. This bill would have required any health plan covering breast cancer treatment to pay for at least 48 hours of inpatient care after a mastectomy and 24 hours after lymph node surgery, unless the patient and her doctor agreed a shorter stay was appropriate. It also barred insurers from penalizing a woman who chose a shorter stay and required plans to tell enrollees about these rights. The bill never got out of committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Breast cancer patients. The bill would have guaranteed them time to recover in the hospital after major cancer surgery, with the decision to go home earlier left to the patient and her doctor rather than to an insurer's cost rules. It would also have protected patients from any coverage penalty if they chose to go home early, and required plans to disclose the guarantee in writing.

how_it_helps.text: Health plans covering breast cancer treatment would have had to provide at least 48 hours of inpatient coverage after a mastectomy and 24 hours after lymph node dissection.
A shorter stay would be allowed only where the attending physician and patient agreed it was appropriate — putting the medical decision with the patient and doctor rather than the plan.
Plans could not change a patient's coverage terms because she chose a shorter stay, and had to notify enrollees of the required coverage in writing.

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and other health plans would have paid for the added hospital days, and those costs would be passed through to employers and premiums. Hospitals would gain additional billed inpatient days.

drawbacks.text: The mandate adds cost: health plans and the employers and families who pay premiums would bear the expense of the required extra hospital days, which critics of coverage mandates argue drives premiums up for everyone.

A fixed 48-hour floor is a blunt instrument; medical practice changed during this era so that some patients were medically ready to go home sooner, though the bill allows the physician and patient to agree to a shorter stay.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is targeted and real: recovery time after major cancer surgery, with the decision left to the patient and her doctor, and no penalty for going home early. The cost is a modest coverage mandate passed through premiums. The physician-and-patient exception blunts the main objection that the floor is one-size-fits-all. On balance a modest, well-designed patient protection.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Commerce Committee, then to its health subcommittee, and sat there until Congress adjourned — it never got a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Rosa DeLauro introduced the Breast Cancer Patient Protection Act of 1996 on September 28, 1996, with 16 original cosponsors.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Commerce on the day it was introduced.
On October 4, 1996, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health and Environment, where it remained with no further action.
The 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997, and the bill died in subcommittee without any vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers and managed care plans were better off: they avoided a requirement to pay for minimum hospital stays after mastectomy surgery, and breast cancer patients got no federal guarantee of recovery time.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Health insurers and managed care plans

for.name: Rosa DeLauro
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the House floor.

for.name: John Dingell, Bernie Sanders, Nancy Pelosi, and 13 other original cosponsors
for.role: U.S. Representatives who cosponsored the bill
for.what_they_did: Signed on as original cosponsors when the bill was introduced.

against.name: Thomas J. Bliley Jr.
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: The committee never acted on the bill; it was referred to the health subcommittee and received no hearing or markup before Congress ended.

against.name: Health insurers and managed care plans
against.role: Health plans covering breast cancer treatment
against.what_they_did: Opposed minimum-stay mandates, which would have required them to pay for longer hospitalizations after mastectomies; their practice of early discharge was the problem the bill targeted.

sides.party_line_note: The 16 cosponsors included 14 Democrats, 1 Independent, and 1 Republican — the bill drew mostly Democratic support but was bipartisan at the margins, and it died in committee without any roll call.

industries.industry: Health insurers and managed care plans
industries.note: The bill would have forced plans to pay for at least 48 hours of inpatient care after a mastectomy, ending the cost-saving practice of discharging women within hours of surgery. Because the industry's savings came directly at recovering patients' expense, its interest ran against the public's in this bill.

The mandate would have meant additional billed inpatient days for surgical patients. Hospitals' interest in the requirement ran alongside patients' interest in recovery time, though longer stays also cost the system more.
